title: ImGui in a Game You Ship
summary: Dear ImGui is a development tool first. Before a game ships, decide what happens to the debug interface - compile it out, hide it behind a key, or keep a few tools for players - and check what it costs. This lesson covers build switches, performance, security and licensing.
markdown:
## Three choices

| Choice | When | How |
|---|---|---|
| **Compile it out** | Most shipped games | A build switch removes every debug window and the ImGui calls |
| **Hidden behind a key or a flag** | Games tested by others, early access | Present but not drawn until a debug key or a command-line flag |
| **Keep some tools for players** | Modding tools, level editors shipped with the game | Treated as real product UI: styled, tested, translated |

## A build switch

Give your project a configuration flag, say `XENON_DEV_TOOLS`, defined in Debug and in an internal "Development" configuration, and not in Shipping:

```cpp-norun
#if XENON_DEV_TOOLS
    drawDebugWindows();
    ImGui::ShowMetricsWindow(&showMetrics);
#endif
```

Keep tool code in its own files (`debug_ui/*.cpp`) so the shipping build can leave whole files out. If the game uses ImGui for nothing else, the shipping build need not link ImGui at all, which also removes the font atlas and its texture memory.

## What it costs

Measure before guessing:

- **CPU**: building the UI runs your code every frame. Debug windows that loop over every entity are the usual culprits; use the clipper and only build windows that are open (lesson 1.04's `Begin` return value).
- **GPU**: usually tiny, a few draw calls. Watch for thousands of custom draw-list primitives.
- **Memory**: the font atlas (a few megabytes with large fonts and icon fonts), plus vertex buffers.
- **Input**: if a debug window has keyboard focus, the game must not react to keys (lesson 2.05). In a shipping build with hidden tools, make sure nothing can grab focus while hidden.

The Metrics window (lesson 1.06) shows vertex counts per window.

## Security and cheating

Debug tools that edit memory, spawn items or teleport are cheats in a multiplayer game. In anything online:

- compile them out of client builds, rather than hiding them;
- never trust the client: the server decides what is allowed, whatever the client's interface can do.

## Licensing

Dear ImGui is under the **MIT licence**: free to use in commercial games, provided the licence text is included with the software (usually in an "open source licences" screen or file). The same goes for ImPlot and most companion libraries; check each one's licence. Fonts have their own licences (Font Awesome Free and most Google Fonts allow embedding with attribution).

## Checklist

- [ ] Shipping configuration builds without `XENON_DEV_TOOLS` and runs.
- [ ] No debug window can be opened in a shipping build by any key combination.
- [ ] Debug-only assets (tool fonts, icon fonts) are not in the shipping package.
- [ ] Licence texts for every library and font are included.
- [ ] For a game with shipped tools: those windows are styled, scale with the display, work with a controller if the game does, and are translated.

## Check yourself
```quiz
? Name the three choices for ImGui in a shipped game.
- Compile it out, replace it with Win32 controls, or move it to a separate process
+ Compile it out, keep it hidden behind a key or flag, or keep some tools as real player-facing features
- Ship it unchanged, ship it with a different style, or ship it only in the Debug build
> Most shipped games compile it out; hidden tools suit test builds, and shipped tools must be treated as real product UI.

? Where does ImGui's cost usually come from?
- GPU time drawing ImGui's vertices, which takes most of a typical frame
- Memory for the copy of every widget's state ImGui keeps between frames
+ CPU time building debug windows each frame, mostly ones that loop over many objects
> The GPU work is usually a few draw calls, and most memory goes to the font atlas. Use the clipper and only build windows that are open.

? What must you check about input when tools are hidden?
- That the hidden windows still receive the keyboard, so they are ready when shown
+ That nothing can take keyboard or mouse focus while hidden, so the game always receives its input
- That `io.WantCaptureKeyboard` is set to true every frame
> If a hidden window kept focus, the game would stop reacting to keys while showing no reason why.

? What should happen to cheat-like debug tools in an online game's client?
- Hide them behind a secret key combination only developers know
- Leave them in, since players are unlikely to ever find them
+ Compile them out, and make sure the server does not trust the client anyway
> Hidden tools can still be found and enabled; compiled-out code cannot. Even then, the server decides what is allowed.

? What does the MIT licence require when you ship Dear ImGui?
- Paying a fee per copy sold
+ Including the licence text with the software
- Publishing your game's source code
> It is a permissive licence: free for commercial use as long as the licence text is included, usually in an "open source licences" screen or file.

? Why put debug UI code in its own files?
- Because ImGui calls only work in separate translation units
- To make the debug windows load faster
+ So the shipping build can leave whole files out
> A build switch is cleaner at the file level, and without the tools the shipping build may not need to link ImGui at all.
```
